periods.analysis: After-school program capacity opened this arc at 90.7%, comfortably above our 85% target and a strong signal that families had real choices when school resumed. With no prior quarter in this series, I read this as a healthy baseline: the Linden, Bayfront, and North Pier community centers were carrying full rosters without turning rooms into holding areas. Site leads used staggered homework tables, gym rotations, and library branch reading corners so capacity translated into safe, useful hours for children, not just seats on a list.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the fall operating model by keeping the shared Parks-Library staffing roster in place at Linden, Bayfront, and North Pier. Extend the waitlist dashboard to show school feeder patterns by bus route, so the next enrollment push reaches families before a site fills. Keep capacity above target while auditing room-use plans for quality, especially homework support and snack service timing.

periods.analysis: Capacity eased from 90.7% to 89.9%, a quarter-over-quarter movement of -0.8 points, but it remained green and well above target. The slight dip looks operational rather than structural: December holidays, basketball setup at Harborview Rec, and early-release-day staffing constraints reduced usable slots on a few afternoons. Families still saw reliable coverage, and the program preserved its basic promise that a working parent should not have to rebuild child care every week.
periods.recommendations: Hold the holiday staffing playbook, but pre-book substitute recreation aides for the two weeks around winter break instead of filling shifts one day at a time. Ask site supervisors to identify rooms that can be converted within 15 minutes after youth sports setup, with Bayfront as the pilot. Maintain the green result by protecting program quality while recovering the few slots lost to seasonal room conflicts.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q1, capacity moved from 89.9% to 88.7%, a -1.2 point change, still green and still meaningfully above the 85% target. The second small decline tells me we should pay attention, not panic: staff certifications, flu-season absences, and the North Pier HVAC repair narrowed usable program hours. We also saw more middle-school demand near the airport employment corridor, which is good news for access but harder to absorb in rooms built for younger cohorts. The resident outcome remains positive, with most families able to find an after-school option close to school or transit.
periods.recommendations: Create a spring micro-credential sprint for part-time recreation aides so CPR, youth mental health, and van-monitor coverage do not become hidden capacity limits. Use the airport corridor demand data to add a targeted middle-school cohort at Seaport Library two days per week. Keep the green performance steady by pairing every facilities work order that affects youth rooms with a temporary relocation plan.

periods.analysis: Capacity declined again from 88.7% to 88.0%, a -0.7 point movement, but remained green. This quarter’s number reflects the tight pre-summer handoff, when school calendars, staff college graduations, and permit checks all land at once. I am encouraged that even with those pressures, our teams kept capacity three points above target and avoided broad waitlist growth. The work at Maple Courts and East Channel showed what good coordination looks like: classroom keys, snack deliveries, and parent pickup zones were solved before the first Monday rush.
periods.recommendations: Lock the Q2-to-summer transition checklist into standard practice, with named owners for permits, food service delivery, and parent communications at every site. Add a weekly April-May capacity huddle for Maple Courts, East Channel, and any site below 87% projected use. Sustain access by publishing confirmed summer-adjacent after-school slots earlier, so families are not left guessing during the school-year close.

periods.analysis: The program rebounded strongly in 2025-Q3, rising from 88.0% to 91.5%, a +3.5 point quarter-over-quarter gain. That is the kind of operational improvement residents can feel: more children placed, fewer parents patching together rides, and better use of city rooms already paid for by the public. The Parks-Library shared cohort model appears to have paid off, especially at Westhaven Library, Bayfront Gym, and the Linden teen room. This is green performance with momentum, not luck.
periods.recommendations: Make the shared cohort model permanent at the three highest-performing sites and document the staffing ratios, room maps, and pickup procedures that drove the +3.5 point improvement. Use ARPA-closeout program funds, where eligible, to purchase portable storage carts and radios so temporary learning spaces can open quickly. Extend the gains by offering principals a September slot-confirmation window tied to school enrollment nights.

periods.analysis: Capacity held nearly flat at a very strong level, moving from 91.5% to 91.2%, a -0.3 point change while staying green. I see this as successful stabilization after the Q3 expansion, because the team kept the new seats operating through holidays, staff vacations, and winter indoor space pressure. Harborview families benefited from consistency, particularly at sites serving shift workers connected to the seaport and airport. The small dip is worth watching only to make sure we are not asking the same supervisors to carry too much overtime.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the expanded capacity by capping recurring overtime and building a bench of trained float staff for Bayfront, Linden, and Westhaven. Run a December after-action review focused on no-show patterns, pickup congestion, and staff fatigue rather than simply counting seats. Preserve the 91% range by converting proven temporary cohorts into posted, budgeted program slots for the next school term.

periods.analysis: In 2026-Q1, capacity fell from 91.2% to 88.5%, a -2.7 point movement, though it remained green and above target. This is the first drop large enough for me to call out directly, and the causes appear manageable: winter illness, two delayed background-check batches, and room displacement during the South Harbor roof repair. Even so, 88.5% means the program continued to serve families well, and staff did not compromise supervision standards to chase a number. Green does not mean effortless; it means the system absorbed stress and still delivered.
periods.recommendations: Treat background-check turnaround as the watch-item and set a five-business-day internal escalation trigger with Human Resources and the vendor. Pre-assign alternate rooms for any facility project affecting youth programs, starting with South Harbor and the Elm Street annex. Sustain the green status by protecting safety ratios first, then restoring lost seats through float staff and short-term library room blocks.

periods.analysis: Capacity improved from 88.5% to 89.1%, a +0.6 point movement, keeping the measure green and showing recovery from the winter disruption. The improvement is modest but meaningful because it came from better execution: faster clearance of aide files, reopening South Harbor rooms, and tighter coordination with school dismissal times. Families saw the benefit in fewer midweek placement changes and more predictable pickup windows. We are not back to the 91% peak yet, but the direction is right and the operating base is sound.
periods.recommendations: Continue the clearance-tracking protocol and publish a monthly staffing readiness report before each registration cycle. Extend the South Harbor recovery model to older sites by pairing facility calendars with program capacity forecasts six weeks in advance. Aim to move back toward the 91% range by adding one flexible cohort at a library or community room in each high-demand feeder area while preserving the quality families count on.

periods.analysis: After-school capacity reached 81.4%, up from June’s recorded 78.9% but 3.6 percentage points below the 85% target. The improvement has not yet produced enough available program capacity for families.
periods.recommendations: Review staffing clearance, room availability and waitlists by site, then identify where a staffed cohort can be added without weakening supervision.
